g.text: Existing compiler infrastructures are powerful, but they assume that every language
can be represented using one common abstraction (one IR or one programming model).
The problem is that some tasks need a different level of abstraction:

The principle is: preserve high-level semantic information
(loops, parallel constructs, tensors, etc.) for as long as it is
useful, lower it only when necessary, and allow multiple abstraction
levels to coexist in the same IR so different parts
of a program can be optimized according to their needs.

MLIR wants transformations, optimizations, and lowering steps
to be expressed as declarative rewrite rules that can be analyzed, composed,
and applied across many abstraction levels instead of being hidden in imperative compiler code.
MLIR wants every operation to retain information about
its origin and transformation history, making compilation
transparent, debuggable, certifiable, and safer for security-critical applications
where optimizations can accidentally invalidate important properties.

—> polyhedral code generation, which is a compiler technique
used to optimize loop-intensive programs (common in scientific
—> MLIR's Affine Dialect provides a simplified polyhedral
representation that preserves loop structure while
supporting affine loops, affine memory accesses, and
structured memory types. Compared to traditional
polyhedral frameworks, it offers richer types, integrates
with SSA-based compiler optimizations, avoids expensive
loop reconstruction, and achieves faster compilation, making
it practical for a wide range of high-performance code
